name: Dark Mauve
lede: Dark mauve is the dusky shade of [[mauve]], and Garfield uses the phrase for the paste that Perkin's dye first became in the factory.

sections.title: The color of the paste
sections.body:
Garfield describes how William Perkin, speaking to the Society of Arts on New Year's Day, walked his audience through the making of mauve [1]. After two days of work, the product was distilled, filtered, washed with caustic soda and water, and left as a very dark mauve paste [1]. Perkin then listed on a chalk board how little dye came from so much coal: from 100 pounds of coal, a mere quarter of an ounce of mauve [1]. He claimed one pound of the dye could color 200 pounds of cotton [1].

So dark mauve names the dye's own strong, concentrated tone, before it was thinned to the paler shades fashion took up. For the full story of the dye and its name see [[mauve]], and for the lighter relatives look at [[plum]], [[dark-purple]] and [[pink]]. Garfield is the only book we use here, and the phrase in his chapter is a description, not a standard name.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This swatch appears in only 17 of 23,781 paintings, 0.07 per cent [2]. The earliest is dated 1560, and the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of the dye, which did not exist until 1856 [2][3].
